document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 42-year-old man is rescued from a house fire with deep partial and full thickness burns to his trunk and both arms. Two large-bore intravenous lines are inserted, Ringer's lactate is started using the Parkland formula, and a Foley catheter is placed. He is intubated for suspected inhalation injury. Which of the following is the best parameter for monitoring the adequacy of his fluid resuscitation?

options.text: Hourly urine output maintained above 0.5 cc/kg/h
Central venous pressure measured every 4 hours
Serial hematocrit measurements
Mean arterial pressure alone, targeting a value above 90 mmHg
Serial body weights every 12 hours

questions.explanation: In acute burn care, urine output is the best measure of resuscitation adequacy and should be maintained at more than 0.5 cc/kg/h in adults (1.0 cc/kg/h in children under 12 yr). This is why a Foley catheter is inserted routinely. A clear sensorium, heart rate below 120/min and mean arterial pressure above 70 mmHg are supportive but secondary endpoints.

optionExplanations.b: Central venous pressure is not listed as a resuscitation endpoint in burn care and is invasive and unreliable in the setting of massive capillary leak.
optionExplanations.c: Hematocrit rises with hemoconcentration but is not the recommended measure of resuscitation adequacy.
optionExplanations.d: Mean arterial pressure is an adjunctive target, and the threshold cited is above 70 mmHg, not 90 mmHg; urine output remains the best measure.
optionExplanations.e: Serial weights are far too slow and imprecise to guide hour-to-hour burn resuscitation.

source.reference: PL21 — Acute Care of Burn Patients

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman has deep partial thickness flame burns to both legs. A topical antimicrobial that penetrates eschar well is applied widely at each dressing change, and she finds the application moderately painful. On day three she becomes tachypneic, and an arterial blood gas shows a metabolic acidosis with no other identifiable cause. Which topical agent most likely explains this finding?

options.text: Silver sulfadiazine cream
Mafenide acetate (Sulfamylon)
Silver nitrate 0.5% solution
Nanocrystalline silver-coated dressing (Acticoat)
Bacitracin-polymyxin (Polysporin) ointment

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists mafenide acetate (Sulfamylon) as moderately painful on application, penetrating eschar well, and capable of causing metabolic acidosis with wide application, along with mild inhibition of epithelialization. The combination of good eschar penetration, painful application, wide use and an otherwise unexplained metabolic acidosis points to this agent.

optionExplanations.a: Silver sulfadiazine causes minimal pain and is associated with leukopenia, slowed healing and pseudoeschar formation, not metabolic acidosis.
optionExplanations.c: Silver nitrate 0.5% is painless with minimal penetration; its characteristic adverse effects are methemoglobinemia, black staining and sodium leaching.
optionExplanations.d: Nanocrystalline silver-coated dressings cause none or transient pain, do not penetrate eschar, and are associated with staining and raised liver enzymes.
optionExplanations.e: Polysporin is used for superficial partial thickness burn dressing changes and is not associated with a systemic acid-base disturbance.

questions.topic: Burn Wound Care and Topical Antimicrobials

source.reference: PL22 — Burn Wound Healing, Table 20: Antimicrobial Dressings for Burns

questions.question: A 28-year-old farm worker sustains a heavily contaminated crush laceration of the thigh with substantial devitalized tissue and presents 14 hours after the injury. In the operating room the wound is irrigated and debrided, then packed open with planned dressing changes and repeat debridement. Suture closure is planned for day five, once healthy granulation tissue has formed and the bacterial burden has fallen. Which type of wound healing does this describe?

options.text: Primary (first intention) healing
Secondary (second intention) healing
Tertiary (delayed primary) healing
Primary closure over a closed suction drain
Immediate coverage with a split thickness skin graft

questions.explanation: Tertiary or delayed primary healing is the intentional interruption of the healing process with packing and sharp debridement, followed by primary closure roughly 4-10 days after injury once granulation tissue has formed and the bacterial count has fallen. It is indicated for contaminated wounds, long time lapse since injury, and severe crush with devitalized tissue, exactly this patient's situation; prolonging the inflammatory phase lowers the bacterial count and the risk of post-closure infection.

optionExplanations.a: Primary closure is contraindicated here: crush injury, heavy contamination and prolonged time since injury are all listed contraindications.
optionExplanations.b: Secondary intention means the wound is left open to heal on its own by contraction and epithelialization, whereas this wound is deliberately closed with sutures on day five.
optionExplanations.d: Placing a drain does not change the fact that immediate closure of a contaminated crush wound is contraindicated, and this is not a recognized category of wound healing.
optionExplanations.e: A graft is a reconstructive option for a granulating bed, not the healing category being described; the plan here is direct suture closure.

questions.topic: Types of Wound Healing and Closure

questions.question: A 68-year-old man has had an open ulcer on his lower leg for three years, arising at the site of an old burn scar. Despite appropriate dressings, treatment of infection and correction of pressure and metabolic factors, it has never healed. Over the past few months the edges have become raised, heaped up and friable, and the wound bleeds easily on dressing changes. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Biopsy of the ulcer to rule out a Marjolin's ulcer
Continue the current dressing regimen and reassess in six weeks
Start empiric oral antibiotics for presumed critical colonization
Apply negative pressure wound therapy to the ulcer
Excise the ulcer and immediately resurface it with a split thickness skin graft

questions.explanation: A chronic wound is one that fails to achieve primary healing within 4-6 weeks, and Toronto Notes specifically advises considering biopsy in non-healing wounds to rule out a Marjolin's ulcer, a squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound because of the chronic inflammatory state. This man's three-year non-healing burn-scar ulcer with newly raised, friable margins is the classic setting, and tissue diagnosis must precede definitive treatment.

optionExplanations.b: Simply continuing an already failed regimen delays the diagnosis of a malignancy that has been developing over months.
optionExplanations.c: There are no described signs of infection, and antibiotics do not address the underlying reason this wound has not healed.
optionExplanations.d: Negative pressure wound therapy is contraindicated over malignant tissue, so malignancy must be excluded first.
optionExplanations.e: Definitive excision and grafting should follow, not precede, histological diagnosis, since a squamous cell carcinoma requires appropriate oncological margins.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman is repeatedly woken at night by numbness and tingling of her right hand, which she relieves by shaking and dangling it. She also has symptoms while driving and holding her phone. Examination shows reduced light touch and two-point discrimination at the tips of the thumb, index and middle fingers, with normal sensation over the skin of the thenar eminence. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Carpal tunnel syndrome
Cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve compression at the elbow)
Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome
De Quervain's tenosynovitis
Cervical radiculopathy

questions.explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome is median nerve compression at the wrist by the flexor retinaculum and is the most common peripheral compression neuropathy, with a female to male ratio of about 4:1. Classically the patient is awakened at night with a numb hand relieved by shaking, dangling or rubbing, with daytime symptoms during wrist flexion activities such as driving or holding a phone. Sensory loss follows the median distribution but spares the thenar eminence skin, because the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel.

optionExplanations.b: Ulnar nerve compression produces numbness of the ring and little fingers and intrinsic weakness, not thumb, index and middle fingertip symptoms.
optionExplanations.c: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome causes paresthesia, pain and weakness of the whole upper limb, often with strenuous overhead work, rather than an isolated nocturnal median distribution pattern.
optionExplanations.d: De Quervain's tenosynovitis causes radial styloid pain with a positive Finkelstein's test, not numbness or loss of two-point discrimination.
optionExplanations.e: Radiculopathy typically produces neck and radiating arm pain in a dermatomal pattern and would not spare only the thenar skin while affecting the fingertips.

questions.question: A 51-year-old man with diabetes presents four days after a splinter injury to the tip of his index finger. The distal pulp is tensely swollen, erythematous and exquisitely tender, and the overlying skin is blanched and clearly under pressure. The finger rests in a normal cascade, passive extension is painless, and there is no tenderness along the flexor sheath. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Incision and drainage of the pulp with cultures and Gram stain, plus antibiotics
Warm soaks, elevation and oral antibiotics alone
Urgent operative irrigation of the flexor tendon sheath
Aspiration and irrigation of the distal interphalangeal joint
Splinting in the position of safety with NSAIDs

questions.explanation: A felon is a subcutaneous abscess in the pulp of a digit, typically multiloculated because of fibrous septae, and trauma such as a puncture or splinter is the most common cause of hand infection. Initial treatment is elevation, warm soaks and antibiotics, but incision and drainage with cultures and Gram stain is indicated when there is an obvious abscess, pressure on the overlying skin, or failure of conservative measures. This patient has a tense pulp with blanching skin under pressure, so drainage is required.

optionExplanations.b: Conservative therapy is appropriate only before an abscess is established; here there is already pressure on the overlying skin, which is an indication for drainage.
optionExplanations.c: Flexor tenosynovitis would show a digit held flexed with fusiform swelling and severe pain on passive extension and sheath tenderness, none of which are present.
optionExplanations.d: There is no evidence of septic arthritis of the distal interphalangeal joint; the collection is in the pulp space.
optionExplanations.e: Splinting and analgesia do not decompress a closed pulp space abscess and risk progression to osteomyelitis of the distal phalanx.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman with long-standing varicose veins has a shallow ulcer with irregular margins just above the medial malleolus. Its base has yellow exudate and granulation tissue, and the surrounding skin is brown and discoloured. Distal pulses are normal. The ulcer aches moderately, worsens when her leg is dependent and improves with elevation, and she has no rest pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Venous stasis ulcer
Arterial (ischemic) ulcer
Diabetic neuropathic ulcer
Pressure ulcer
Acute traumatic ulcer

questions.explanation: Venous ulcers account for the majority of vascular ulcers and result from valvular incompetence and venous hypertension. They sit at the medial malleolus in the gaiter area, are superficial with irregular margins, show yellow exudate and granulation tissue, have brown venous stasis discolouration of surrounding skin and normal distal pulses, and are moderately painful with pain increasing on dependency and decreasing on elevation. Treatment is rest, leg elevation, compression and moist dressings, provided the ankle-brachial index is safe for compression.

optionExplanations.b: Arterial ulcers are deep with even punched-out margins, a pale necrotic base, thin shiny hairless skin, absent or diminished pulses, rest pain, and pain that worsens with elevation.
optionExplanations.c: Diabetic ulcers occur at pressure points such as the metatarsal heads, have a necrotic base and hyperkeratotic border, and are typically painless due to neuropathy.
optionExplanations.d: Pressure ulcers develop over bony prominences from sustained pressure reducing tissue perfusion, most often on the lower torso, and are not related to leg dependency.
optionExplanations.e: An acute traumatic ulcer follows an identifiable injury with a failure of the wound to heal; this three-feature picture of varicosities, gaiter location and stasis pigmentation is venous.

source.reference: PL17 — Lower Limb Ulcers, Table 14: Venous vs. Arterial vs. Diabetic Ulcers

questions.question: A 22-year-old man is struck in the right eye by a baseball. He has periorbital ecchymosis and subconjunctival hemorrhage, the globe appears intact and visual acuity is preserved. He cannot elevate the right eye past the neutral position, has diplopia on straight gaze, and develops severe pain and vomiting when he attempts to look upward. The right cheek is numb. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: CT of the orbits with fine slices and urgent referral for operative release of the entrapped muscle
Ice, decongestants and reassessment in 10 days for persistent diplopia
Plain facial radiographs with routine outpatient ophthalmology follow-up
Immediate lateral canthotomy and cantholysis
Bedside forced duction testing without anesthesia to confirm the diagnosis

questions.explanation: Blunt force to the orbit raises intraorbital pressure and can produce a blow-out fracture of the orbital floor with infraorbital nerve (CN V2) anesthesia. Orbital entrapment is a clinical diagnosis and a surgical emergency, signalled by diplopia on straight gaze with inability to look up past neutral due to inferior rectus entrapment, and severe pain or nausea and vomiting on upward globe movement. CT of the orbits with axial, coronal and sagittal fine slices is the diagnostic study, and entrapment is an indication for surgical repair.

optionExplanations.b: Waiting is appropriate only for diplopia without entrapment; surgical repair is indicated for persistent diplopia beyond about 10 days, but frank entrapment cannot be observed.
optionExplanations.c: Plain films are inadequate for the orbit, and routine follow-up would delay emergency surgical release.
optionExplanations.d: Canthotomy and cantholysis treat orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar hematoma, which would present with proptosis and loss of vision, not preserved acuity with restricted upgaze.
optionExplanations.e: The forced duction test is performed with forceps under general anesthesia in the operating room, not at the bedside on an awake patient.

questions.question: A 29-year-old man lacerates the volar aspect of his right ring finger on broken glass. Bleeding is controlled and the digit is well perfused with normal sensation. He can still bend the finger at the proximal interphalangeal joint, but he cannot bend the tip of the finger at the distal interphalangeal joint at all. Which structure has most likely been divided?

options.text: Flexor digitorum superficialis tendon
Flexor digitorum profundus tendon
Flexor pollicis longus tendon
Flexor carpi radialis tendon
Palmaris longus tendon

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that flexor digitorum profundus crosses both the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints while flexor digitorum superficialis crosses only the proximal interphalangeal joint, since deeper tendons extend more distally than superficial tendons. Loss of distal interphalangeal flexion with preserved proximal interphalangeal flexion therefore localizes the division to the profundus tendon. Flexor tendon injuries should be seen and treated sooner than extensor injuries because of the risk of retraction.

optionExplanations.a: Flexor digitorum superficialis crosses only the proximal interphalangeal joint, so its division would abolish proximal interphalangeal flexion, which is preserved here.
optionExplanations.c: Flexor pollicis longus flexes the thumb and has no action on the ring finger.
optionExplanations.d: Flexor carpi radialis inserts on the metacarpal bases and flexes the wrist; it does not flex the digits.
optionExplanations.e: Palmaris longus inserts into the palmar aponeurosis and contributes to wrist flexion, not to flexion of the distal interphalangeal joint.

source.reference: PL4 — Hand Anatomy: Flexor Tendons and Carpal Tunnel

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman has a split thickness skin graft placed on a clean granulating wound of the lower leg. The graft is secured with staples and a pressure dressing. Twenty-four hours later the graft is adherent and viable, but no vascular connections have yet formed between the graft and the recipient bed. Which process is sustaining the graft at this point?

options.text: Plasmatic imbibition
Inosculation
Neovascular ingrowth
Primary contraction
Secondary contraction

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes three phases of skin graft take: plasmatic imbibition, the diffusion of nutrition from the recipient site during the first 48 h; inosculation, the growth of vessels from bed and graft toward each other on days 2-3; and neovascular ingrowth, the growth of new vessels that vascularize the graft on days 3-5. At 24 hours, before any vascular connection exists, the graft is surviving by diffusion of nutrients, that is, plasmatic imbibition.

optionExplanations.b: Inosculation, the growth of vessels from bed and graft toward each other, occurs on days 2-3, not in the first 24 hours.
optionExplanations.c: Neovascular ingrowth occurs on days 3-5 and is the phase in which new vessels actually vascularize the graft.
optionExplanations.d: Primary contraction is the immediate reduction in graft size on harvesting, not a mechanism of graft nutrition.
optionExplanations.e: Secondary contraction is reduction in size after the graft is placed on the wound bed and healing has occurred; it does not nourish the graft.

source.reference: PL13 — Partial Thickness Skin Graft Survival

questions.question: A 38-year-old man spills boiling oil over himself. He has many small scattered patches of deep partial thickness burn over the chest, abdomen and left arm, each separated by normal uninjured skin, plus a broad area of blanchable erythema. He is alert and haemodynamically stable. Which is the most appropriate way to estimate the percentage of total body surface area burned?

options.text: Rule of 9s applied to each involved anatomical region
Surface area of the patient's palm with fingers adducted, taken as approximately 1% of total body surface area
Lund-Browder chart
Modified Baux score
Estimation from the etiologic agent and duration of exposure

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that for patchy burns the surface area covered by the patient's palm with the fingers adducted represents approximately 1% of total body surface area. The rule of 9s is intended for contiguous superficial partial, deep partial and full thickness burns and overestimates scattered patches. Note also that total body surface area does not include areas with superficial burns, so the blanchable erythema is excluded.

optionExplanations.a: The rule of 9s assigns whole anatomical regions and cannot accurately sum many small separated patches.
optionExplanations.c: The Lund-Browder chart is used in children under 10 yr to account for changing body proportions with age.
optionExplanations.d: The modified Baux score predicts mortality once burn size and age are known; it does not measure burn size.
optionExplanations.e: History of the etiologic agent and time of exposure helps assess burn depth, not the surface area involved.

source.reference: PL19 — Diagnosis and Prognosis: Burn Size Estimation

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman is assessed after a scald injury to her thigh. The burned skin has a mottled appearance, is only minimally painful, and is less blanchable than the surrounding skin. It is softer than a leathery eschar, and some hair follicles remain attached. Which burn depth best describes this injury?

options.text: Erythema/superficial (first degree)
Superficial partial thickness (second degree)
Deep partial thickness (second degree)
Full thickness (third degree)
Fourth degree

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes characterizes a deep partial thickness burn, extending into the deep reticular dermis, as minimally painful, difficult to distinguish from full thickness, mottled in appearance, less blanchable, softer than a full thickness burn, and with some hair follicles still attached. Every one of those features is present here, which places the injury in the deep dermis rather than the superficial dermis or beyond.

optionExplanations.a: A superficial burn is confined to the epidermis and is painful, erythematous and blanchable with sensation intact.
optionExplanations.b: A superficial partial thickness burn extends into the papillary dermis and is painful and blanchable with blisters containing clear fluid.
optionExplanations.d: A full thickness burn is insensate with a hard leathery eschar that is black, grey, white or cherry red, and hairs do not stay attached.
optionExplanations.e: Fourth degree burns involve underlying tissue structures such as muscle and bone.

questions.question: A 27-year-old man had his forearm compressed between two industrial rollers five hours ago. The forearm is tense and the pain is far worse than expected, particularly on passive stretch of the fingers. He reports paresthesia in the hand. The limb is warm and the radial pulse remains palpable. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Emergent fasciotomy
Needle manometry of the compartment, operating only if the pressure exceeds 30-40 mmHg
Elevate the limb above the heart and reassess in four hours
Doppler ultrasound of the radial and ulnar arteries
Splint the forearm and obtain x-rays before any further decision

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that the indication for an emergent fasciotomy in compartment syndrome is based on the clinical diagnosis: a tense, painful extremity that is worse on passive stretch, with paresthesia or paralysis, pallor and distal pulselessness, the last being often late in the process. Intracompartmental pressures can be measured but vary between limbs and with comorbidities, so a preserved pulse does not exclude the diagnosis. If untreated the end result is ischemic contracture of the extremity (Volkmann's contracture).

optionExplanations.b: Measured pressures vary between upper and lower extremity and with comorbidities, so waiting for a numerical threshold before operating risks irreversible ischemia.
optionExplanations.c: Elevation and observation in an already tense, exquisitely painful compartment allows the ischemic injury to progress.
optionExplanations.d: Distal pulselessness is often a late finding, so a Doppler study of the radial and ulnar arteries cannot rule out compartment syndrome.
optionExplanations.e: Splinting a tense compartment and delaying for imaging postpones the only treatment that prevents Volkmann's contracture.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presents three days after a penetrating injury to the volar aspect of his middle finger. The whole digit is uniformly fusiform swollen and is held in a flexed posture. There is point tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath and severe pain on passive extension of the digit. He is febrile, and frank pus drains when the entry wound is probed. What is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Oral antibiotics with a resting hand splint and elevation
Incision and drainage in the operating room
Warm compresses with oral antibiotics
Oral acyclovir
Nail plate removal

questions.explanation: The four Kanavel cardinal signs of infectious flexor tenosynovitis are point tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath, pain on passive extension, fusiform swelling of the digit, and a flexed posture of the digit. Toronto Notes directs that non-suppurative disease be treated with antibiotics, a resting hand splint and elevation, whereas suppurative disease that produces pus requires incision and drainage in the operating room. This patient has all four signs plus frank pus, so operative drainage is needed to prevent tendon necrosis and rupture.

optionExplanations.a: Antibiotics, splinting and elevation are the treatment for the non-suppurative form; they are insufficient once pus is present.
optionExplanations.c: Warm compresses with oral antibiotics is the early treatment of acute paronychia, an infection of the soft tissue around the fingernail.
optionExplanations.d: Acyclovir is considered for severe herpetic whitlow, which presents as painful vesicles around the fingertip rather than a fusiform swollen digit with pus.
optionExplanations.e: Nail plate removal is used when a paronychial abscess extends beneath the nail plate, not for infection within the flexor tendon sheath.

questions.question: A 21-year-old volleyball player takes a sudden blow to the tip of her extended right middle finger. The distal interphalangeal joint now rests in flexion and she has lost active extension at that joint, although passive extension is full. Radiographs show no fracture of the distal phalanx. What is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Splint the distal interphalangeal joint in extension continuously for 6 weeks
Splint the proximal interphalangeal joint in extension with active distal interphalangeal motion for 6 weeks
Two weeks of night splinting only
Steroid injection into the tendon sheath
Tendon rebalancing or arthrodesis

questions.explanation: Mallet finger is a distal interphalangeal joint held in flexion with loss of active extension, and the non-bony form follows forced flexion of the extended distal interphalangeal joint such as a sudden blow to the fingertip, rupturing the extensor tendon. Toronto Notes treats this by splinting the distal interphalangeal joint in extension for 6 weeks with no exception, since even one episode of flexion requires the patient to restart, followed by 2 weeks of night splinting.

optionExplanations.b: Splinting the proximal interphalangeal joint in extension while allowing active distal interphalangeal motion is the treatment of boutonniere deformity from a central slip injury.
optionExplanations.c: Night splinting is only the 2 week phase that follows the initial 6 weeks of continuous extension splinting; used alone it is inadequate.
optionExplanations.d: Steroid injection into the tendon sheath is used for De Quervain's tenosynovitis, not for a ruptured terminal extensor tendon.
optionExplanations.e: Tendon rebalancing or arthrodesis is a corrective procedure for established swan neck deformity, not initial treatment of an acute mallet injury.

questions.question: A 23-year-old office clerk punched a wall and has pain and swelling over the ulnar border of his hand. There is loss of prominence of the fifth metacarpal head when he makes a fist. Radiographs show a fracture through the neck of the fifth metacarpal with 25 degrees of volar angulation. There is no malrotation or scissoring of the fingers, and the fracture is stable. What is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Ulnar gutter splint for 3-4 weeks with early protected range of motion
Closed reduction followed by splinting
Percutaneous pinning with K-wires
Open reduction and internal fixation
Buddy taping to the ring finger with immediate unrestricted use

questions.explanation: A boxer's fracture is an acute fracture of the neck of the fifth metacarpal caused by impact with a closed fist, producing loss of prominence of the metacarpal head and volar displacement of the head into the palm. Toronto Notes reserves closed reduction for angulation greater than 40 degrees, rotation, or manual labourers with painful grip, and otherwise treats a stable fracture with an ulnar gutter splint for 3-4 weeks with early protected range of motion.

optionExplanations.b: Closed reduction is considered for angulation greater than 40 degrees, rotational deformity, or manual labourers; this fracture meets none of those criteria.
optionExplanations.c: Percutaneous pinning is used for fractures that are displaced, non-reducible, unstable with closed reduction, or rotationally deformed.
optionExplanations.d: Open reduction and internal fixation is reserved for indications such as intra-articular fractures, malrotation, shortening greater than 3-5 mm or extensor lag.
optionExplanations.e: Buddy taping to a neighbouring stable digit is used for non-displaced phalanx fractures and would leave this metacarpal neck fracture unprotected.

source.reference: PL28 — Fractures and Dislocations: Metacarpal Fractures

questions.question: A 31-year-old man is assaulted and sustains a high velocity blow to the face. He has facial asymmetry with depression of the right cheek bone, a palpable step deformity of the infraorbital rim, malocclusion and a tender mandible. His airway is patent, visual acuity and extraocular movements are normal, and he is hemodynamically stable. Which is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: CT facial bones with 1.5 mm axial, coronal and sagittal slices
CT head
Panorex radiograph
Plain radiographs of the facial bones
Defer imaging and obtain a CT in 3-5 days once the swelling has improved

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes names CT of the facial bones the gold standard investigation for facial trauma, requesting 1.5 mm axial, coronal and sagittal slices, and indicates it for significant head trauma, suspected facial fractures and preoperative assessment. This patient has clinical signs of fractures of both the middle and lower face, so a study that images the whole facial skeleton is required.

optionExplanations.b: A CT head is typically insufficient because its slices are wider and it does not capture the lower mid-face and mandible.
optionExplanations.c: A panorex radiograph shows the upper and lower jaw and is indicated for an isolated mandible fracture in a patient able to sit; it would miss the midface injury.
optionExplanations.d: Plain radiographs do not adequately delineate the facial buttresses and are not the gold standard for facial fractures.
optionExplanations.e: Waiting 3-5 d for swelling to settle applies to reassessing the need for operative treatment, not to obtaining the diagnostic study in a patient with obvious fractures.

source.reference: PL32 — Approach to Facial Injuries: Investigations

questions.question: A 58-year-old man of northern European background reports a firm, painless nodule in his right palm that has slowly developed into a thick fibrous cord running to the ring finger. He can no longer place all his fingers flat against a table simultaneously. Examination shows a 45 degree fixed flexion contracture at the ring finger metacarpophalangeal joint. Active and passive digital flexion are full. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Corticosteroid injection into the palmar nodule
Needle aponeurotomy of the cord
Fasciectomy with excision of the diseased palmar fascia
Injection of Clostridium histolyticum collagenase
Release of the flexor tendon sheath of the ring finger

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists surgical management of Dupuytren's disease for a metacarpophalangeal contracture greater than 30 degrees, a proximal interphalangeal contracture of any degree, significant webspace contracture, functional or hygiene impairment, or a positive Hueston's tabletop test. This man has a 45 degree metacarpophalangeal contracture and cannot place his fingers flat against a table, so excision of the diseased fascia is indicated. Metacarpophalangeal joints have better outcomes than proximal interphalangeal joints after treatment.

optionExplanations.a: Steroid injection is part of non-surgical management, which is indicated for palmar pits, nodules, or simple cords rather than an established contracture beyond 30 degrees.
optionExplanations.b: Needle aponeurotomy is also non-surgical management reserved for pits, nodules, or simple cords, not for a fixed metacarpophalangeal contracture of this size.
optionExplanations.d: Clostridium histolyticum collagenase is listed with the other non-surgical options for pits, nodules, or simple cords, and does not excise the diseased fascia.
optionExplanations.e: Dupuytren's disease is a proliferative disorder of the palmar fascia and the flexor tendons are not involved, so releasing the tendon sheath would not correct the contracture.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman is 18 hours after free flap reconstruction of a lower leg defect using tissue harvested with a named artery and vein and anastomosed microsurgically. The flap skin has turned purple-blue. It remains warm, capillary refill is brisk at under two seconds, and the tissue feels firm and stiff on palpation. An arterial pulse is still audible on Doppler over the pedicle. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Arterial insufficiency of the flap
Venous insufficiency of the flap
Normal, healthy free flap
Erysipelas of the flap skin
Acute rejection of transplanted allograft tissue

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes tabulates the characteristics of a healthy free flap against arterial and venous insufficiency. Venous insufficiency gives a purple or blue colour, a flap that is warm or cool, increased turgor with tissue firmness and stiffness, and capillary refill under 2 seconds. This flap matches that pattern with a preserved arterial Doppler signal, indicating obstructed venous outflow rather than arterial inflow failure.

optionExplanations.a: Arterial insufficiency produces a pale, cool flap with decreased tissue firmness, capillary refill greater than 5 seconds, and loss of the arterial Doppler pulse.
optionExplanations.c: A normal flap is pink and warm, soft but with some firmness, and has capillary refill of 2 to 5 seconds, not a purple-blue congested appearance.
optionExplanations.d: Erysipelas is an acute infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics producing intense raised erythema and induration with sharply demarcated borders, not blue discolouration with brisk refill.
optionExplanations.e: Acute rejection is a concern in vascularized composite allotransplantation from a deceased donor; an autologous free flap of the patient's own tissue is not rejected.

questions.question: An 80-year-old woman with advanced dementia, immobility, and incontinence in long-term care is found to have a sacral pressure injury. The wound base is entirely covered by thick yellow slough and adherent black eschar, so the extent of tissue damage cannot be confirmed on inspection. The surrounding skin is intact. Which classification best describes this pressure injury?

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury
Stage 3 pressure injury
Stage 4 pressure injury
Unstageable pressure injury
Deep tissue pressure injury

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines an unstageable pressure injury as one in which the extent of tissue damage cannot be confirmed because it is obscured by slough or eschar; once debridement is completed the pressure injury can be appropriately staged. That is exactly the situation here. Management then follows the principles of pressure relief, treatment of underlying medical issues, moisture reduction, and wound bed preparation and treatment.

optionExplanations.a: A numbered stage cannot be assigned while slough and eschar obscure the wound base and the extent of tissue damage is unconfirmed.
optionExplanations.b: Assigning this stage would require visualising the depth of tissue damage, which is impossible until debridement is completed.
optionExplanations.c: This also requires direct visualisation of the depth of the injury, which the overlying eschar prevents.
optionExplanations.e: A deep tissue pressure injury is persistent non-blanchable deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration, not a wound base covered by slough and eschar.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man is thrown from his motorcycle and sustains a closed traction and stretch injury of the right brachial plexus. He has weakness of shoulder abduction and elbow flexion with patchy sensory loss in the limb. There is no open wound, no expanding mass such as a hematoma, and no clinical feature suggesting preganglionic root avulsion. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate exploration of the plexus in the operating room
Splinting with occupational therapy and physiotherapy, following for 3-4 months for improvement
Nerve transfer now using an intercostal nerve as donor
EMG and nerve conduction studies immediately to guide urgent repair
CT myelogram now to plan root repair

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that closed traction or stretch injuries of the brachial plexus should be followed for 3-4 months for improvement if there is no continued insult, and that all brachial plexus injuries require splinting plus occupational therapy and physiotherapy consults to maintain range of motion and joint function. Concussive or compressive closed injuries are often self-resolving unless there is an expanding mass such as a hematoma.

optionExplanations.a: Immediate exploration in the operating room is reserved for open injuries with sharp or vascular injury, not for a closed traction injury.
optionExplanations.c: Nerve transfers are indicated when the nerve injury is close to the effector muscle or when other reconstructive options are not possible, such as preganglionic root avulsion or complete loss of motor and sensory function.
optionExplanations.d: EMG and nerve conduction studies are obtained about 12 weeks post-injury to assess healing progress in closed injuries, not immediately.
optionExplanations.e: CT myelogram or MRI is obtained initially in a closed injury when avulsion is suspected, which is not the case here.

source.reference: PL31 — Brachial Plexus Injuries and Nerve Transfers

questions.question: A 5-month-old girl has an isolated complete cleft of the hard and soft palate identified at birth. Her lip is intact. She has fed adequately using special bottles and has already had two episodes of otitis media. She is growing appropriately and has no other congenital anomalies. What is the most appropriate definitive management of her palate?

options.text: Millard or Fisher repair at 3 months of age
Von Langenbeck repair or Furlow Z-plasty at 6-9 months of age
Craniectomy involving a multidisciplinary craniofacial team
Special bottles for feeding and speech-language pathology without operative repair
Myringotomy tube insertion as the definitive procedure

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes gives surgery at 6-9 months, by Von Langenbeck repair or Furlow Z-plasty, as the treatment of cleft palate, alongside speech-language pathology and an ENT consult because recurrent otitis media often requires myringotomy tubes. Isolated cleft palate occurs in about 0.5 in 1000 births and is more common in females, matching this infant.

optionExplanations.a: Millard and Fisher are the repairs listed for cleft lip and are performed at about 3 months; this infant has an intact lip.
optionExplanations.c: Craniectomy with a multidisciplinary team is the treatment of craniosynostosis, a different craniofacial anomaly.
optionExplanations.d: Special bottles for feeding and speech-language pathology are supportive measures listed for cleft lip and palate, but they do not close the palatal cleft.
optionExplanations.e: Myringotomy tubes address the recurrent otitis media that accompanies cleft palate but do not repair the cleft itself.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man is struck on the side of the nose during a hockey game. He has epistaxis, deviation and flattening of the nose, swelling, periorbital ecchymosis, and tenderness over the nasal dorsum. Anterior rhinoscopy shows a bluish, fluctuant swelling bulging from both sides of the nasal septum, and he reports respiratory obstruction. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Closed reduction with Asch forceps under anesthesia, then packing of both nostrils
Small incision in the septal mucosa to drain the collection, followed by packing
Application of an external nasal splint for 7 days
Rhinoplasty deferred until the swelling subsides in 5-7 days
Non-adhesive gauze packing of both nostrils alone

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes directs that a nasal fracture be inspected for a septal hematoma, which must be drained because it is a potential cause of septal necrosis and perforation; drainage is completed with a small incision in the septal mucosa followed by packing. The bluish, fluctuant bilateral septal swelling here is a septal hematoma, so drainage takes precedence over correcting the external deformity. The fracture itself is treated for airway or cosmetic issues once the hematoma is dealt with.

optionExplanations.a: Closed reduction with Asch or Walsham forceps is the treatment for the displaced bony deformity and is best done immediately, but it leaves an undrained septal hematoma to necrose and perforate.
optionExplanations.c: A nasal splint, like petroleum or non-adhesive gauze packing, is part of aftercare following reduction and does not evacuate a septal hematoma.
optionExplanations.d: Rhinoplasty is reserved for residual deformity later on, and delaying any intervention 5-7 days allows septal necrosis and perforation to develop.
optionExplanations.e: Packing alone is used after reduction or drainage; without an incision to evacuate the hematoma the collection remains under the septal mucosa.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman presents with sudden onset swelling of the left breast over 3 weeks, with mild pain but no fever or erythema. She had bilateral macro-textured silicone implants placed subglandularly for augmentation 7 years ago. Imaging shows a large periprosthetic fluid collection with an intact implant shell and a firm mass adjacent to the capsule. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Capsular contracture
Implant failure with rupture and silicone extravasation
Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma
Systemic symptoms associated with breast implants (breast implant illness)
Periprosthetic infection

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma is associated with textured breast implants, with incidence varying by type of texturization from 1/3565 for macro-textured implants, and that it commonly presents as sudden onset breast swelling +/- pain, on average 7-8 yr after implant placement. This woman's macro-textured implants, the 7-year interval, and the abrupt unilateral swelling with a periprosthetic collection and an associated mass fit that presentation. Management is total capsulectomy and excision of the associated mass with bilateral implant removal, with fluid sent for C&S and lymphoma protocol (CD30+, ALK-), and outcome is favourable if detected and treated early.

optionExplanations.a: Capsular contracture is a listed complication of augmentation and is linked to periareolar and transaxillary incisions, but it causes progressive firmness and distortion of the breast rather than sudden swelling with a periprosthetic effusion and mass.
optionExplanations.b: Implant failure/rupture is a recognized complication, but the shell is intact on imaging and rupture does not produce an associated capsular mass requiring lymphoma protocol.
optionExplanations.d: Systemic symptoms associated with breast implants, also called breast implant illness, is a constellation of systemic complaints, not a unilateral late effusion with a discrete mass.
optionExplanations.e: Infection is a listed complication of breast augmentation, but there is no fever or erythema, and infection would not explain a firm mass adjacent to the capsule 7 years after placement.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with diabetes has a rapidly spreading erythematous swelling of the left thigh over 12 hours. He reports pain out of proportion to the clinical findings that extends beyond the border of the erythema. There are scattered blisters and ecchymoses, and crepitus is palpable over the medial thigh. His temperature is 38.9°C and heart rate 122 beats/min. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: CT scan of the thigh to assess for gas in the subcutaneous tissues
Calculate the LRINEC score and admit for serial observation
Emergent surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue
IV cefazolin with the area of erythema outlined to monitor progression
Bedside incision with fascial biopsy and STAT Gram stain

questions.explanation: Necrotizing fasciitis is an aggressive infection of a fascial plane allowing diffuse and rapid spread with secondary necrosis, and it is a life/limb-threatening infection that requires emergent surgical debridement. Toronto Notes states that if there is high clinical suspicion of necrotizing fasciitis, surgical treatment should not be delayed for imaging. Pain disproportionate to clinical findings and beyond the border of erythema, with blistering, ecchymoses and crepitus in a diabetic patient, is the classic picture, so this patient goes emergently to the operating room for removal of all necrotic tissue and copious irrigation, with plans for repeat surgery in 24-48 h alongside vigorous resuscitation and IV antibiotics.

optionExplanations.a: XR or CT can show gas in the subcutaneous tissues, but with high clinical suspicion surgical treatment should not be delayed for imaging.
optionExplanations.b: Necrotizing fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis and the LRINEC score is only a supportive tool; observation permits the diffuse, rapid spread and secondary necrosis that make this infection limb-threatening.
optionExplanations.d: Outlining the erythema and giving cefazolin is the approach to cellulitis; it does not address necrosis within the fascial plane, which needs debridement.
optionExplanations.e: Bedside incision with fascial biopsy and STAT Gram stain is diagnostic but is used in equivocal cases where clinical features are not supportive or the exam is difficult, not when suspicion is already high.
